findings.claim: In Node.js, the global fetch() has been available without a flag since v18.0.0 and has not been experimental since v21.0.0. It is built on the bundled undici HTTP/1.1 client, and the bundled version can be read from process.versions.undici. A Node 22 or 24 CLI can therefore use fetch with no third-party dependency.
findings.falsifier: The Node 22 or 24 docs or changelog marking fetch as experimental, putting it behind a flag, or removing it.
limitations: The 'latest' globals page was read, not the v22- or v24-specific pages.
The fetch section has no per-API stability marker; only the page-level 'Stability: 2 - Stable' was seen.
The bundled undici version differs between Node releases and was not checked.

findings.claim: Node.js 22 (Jod) and 24 (Krypton) are both listed as LTS release lines on the official Node.js releases page, so both are reasonable targets for a production CLI.
findings.falsifier: The Node.js Release schedule (nodejs/Release on GitHub) showing either line as end-of-life or not LTS as of October 2026.
limitations: The page said only 'LTS'; whether each line is Active or Maintenance LTS was not confirmed.
Dates in the page's 'Last updated' column were not treated as end-of-life dates.
The nodejs/Release schedule was not fetched.

findings.claim: A fetch() promise resolves, rather than rejects, on HTTP error statuses such as 404 or 5xx. It rejects only on network or request failures. A CLI using fetch must check response.ok or response.status itself before calling response.json().
findings.falsifier: Node or undici documentation or tests showing that Node's fetch rejects on non-2xx statuses.
limitations: MDN documents the WHATWG/browser behaviour; Node follows the same spec, but no Node-specific page was fetched to confirm this.
Behaviour when response.json() is called on a non-JSON error body was not examined.

findings.claim: By default, Axios rejects the promise when the status code is outside 200–299. Its validateStatus option overrides which codes reject. A rejected error carries error.response (data, status, headers) when the server replied, and error.request (an http.ClientRequest in Node) when no response arrived.
findings.falsifier: Axios source (lib/core/settle.js or defaults) or release notes showing a different default for validateStatus.
limitations: axios-http.com/docs/handling_errors 301-redirected to axios.rest. That page carries 'axios collective' branding but does not explicitly call itself official.
The page was not tied to a specific Axios version.

findings.claim: Axios parses JSON responses into response.data and supports a responseType option. In Node, its default adapter is 'http' (Node's http module), not fetch, although 'fetch' is offered as a built-in adapter alternative.
findings.falsifier: Axios docs or source showing that the Node default adapter is fetch, or that JSON is not parsed automatically by default.
limitations: The fetched page did not state the default responseType; the claim that JSON is parsed automatically rests on the general Axios transformResponse behaviour, not on a quote.
Same origin as the other Axios findings, so not independent.

findings.claim: Neither client has a short default overall deadline. Axios's 'timeout' option is a millisecond request timeout. Node's fetch has no timeout option of its own, and the undici Client defaults are headersTimeout 300e3 ms, bodyTimeout 300e3 ms and connectTimeout 10e3 ms. A CLI needing a firm deadline should set one explicitly, e.g. with AbortSignal.timeout(ms).
findings.falsifier: Evidence that Node's global fetch uses a dispatcher whose timeout defaults differ from the undici Client defaults, or that the Axios timeout covers the whole transfer including the body.
limitations: These are the defaults on undici's main branch; the undici versions bundled in Node 22/24 may differ.
Whether the Axios timeout is a total deadline or an idle/socket timeout in the http adapter was not confirmed from the docs.
The Axios timeout description came from axios.rest (request-config page).

findings.claim: Node provides AbortSignal.timeout(delay), added in v17.3.0, and AbortSignal.any(signals), added in v20.3.0. Both are available in Node 22 and 24, so a fetch-based CLI can combine a deadline with user cancellation (e.g. Ctrl+C) in one signal. A timeout aborts with a 'TimeoutError' DOMException, which is distinct from 'AbortError'.
findings.falsifier: Node runtime behaviour showing AbortSignal.timeout aborting with AbortError instead of TimeoutError, or AbortSignal.any being unavailable in Node 22/24.
limitations: The TimeoutError vs AbortError naming comes from MDN (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal/timeout_static), a separate origin.
Whether the signal also aborts an in-progress body read (response.json()) is not stated explicitly on either page.

findings.claim: Axios has supported cancellation through AbortController's signal option since v0.22.0. Its older CancelToken API is deprecated and slated for removal in the next major release, so both clients cancel through the same AbortSignal mechanism.
findings.falsifier: Axios release notes showing CancelToken un-deprecated, or signal unsupported in the http adapter.
limitations: The page does not discuss AbortSignal.timeout or AbortSignal.any with Axios; compatibility was inferred, not confirmed.
axios.rest is reached by redirect from axios-http.com; its official status is inferred.

findings.claim: Axios is a third-party dependency with its own transitive runtime dependencies. The v1.x package.json (version 1.20.0) declares follow-redirects, form-data, https-proxy-agent and proxy-from-env. Built-in fetch adds zero npm dependencies.
findings.falsifier: The published npm tarball for the release used declaring a different set of dependencies.
limitations: This is the v1.x branch head, not necessarily the version on npm today.
The full transitive tree size and install footprint were not measured.

Built-in fetch does not honour HTTP(S)_PROXY env vars by default (undici needs an explicit ProxyAgent/EnvHttpProxyAgent); this was not checked here and is a possible advantage for Axios's proxy-from-env support.

findings.claim: Taking a dependency carries supply-chain risk, and Axios has a concrete incident. On 2026-03-31, malicious axios versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 were published from a compromised maintainer account. They added a plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 dependency whose postinstall script downloaded a cross-platform payload. Advisory GHSA-fw8c-xr5c-95f9 says to treat affected systems as fully compromised; 1.14.0 and 0.30.3 are safe.
findings.falsifier: The GitHub Advisory Database or the axios maintainers retracting or materially correcting the advisory.
limitations: Corroborated by the Singapore CSA advisory AD-2026-002 (https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/advisories/ad-2026-002/), seen only in search results and not fetched.
The GitHub-hosted GHSA page and any axios maintainer post-mortem were not fetched.
One past incident does not quantify ongoing risk; lockfiles, pinned versions and --ignore-scripts reduce exposure.

findings.claim: Conditional recommendation (inferred from the findings above): for a Node 22/24 CLI making simple JSON GET requests, prefer built-in fetch wrapped in a small helper. The helper should check response.ok and throw a typed error with the status and body, and pass signal: AbortSignal.any([AbortSignal.timeout(ms), userController.signal]). Choose Axios when the codebase already uses it, when it needs interceptors or instance defaults, automatic env-based proxying, or auto-reject on non-2xx without writing a wrapper. In that case pin it with a lockfile and audit it, given the March 2026 compromise.
findings.falsifier: Benchmarks or bug reports showing Node fetch with AbortSignal deadlines is unreliable in Node 22/24, or that Axios offers a deadline or cancellation capability fetch cannot replicate.
limitations: This is a synthesis of the other findings, not a sourced statement.
Performance, retries, streaming, cookie handling and proxy behaviour were not compared.
Behaviour was not verified by running code.
